**SECTION ONE: LOGIC**

**1.** *Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow:*

> Chris tried to get up but he couldn't because the pain was very sharp. If he shows any sign of pain, then he will be kicked out of the team. He knew he could not afford to lose the scholarship. Some pains are difficult to hide. That is why the coach had to notice it.
>
> It was the championship game and he did not want to miss it. The coach told him "If he stays and plays then he will die in the field and if he fails to see the doctor then he will die in the field". Chris replied with a smile "if Jones can play with a broken leg, so can I".

**Questions**
incertitudes: Q1(a)(iii) : le sujet demande « la converse du contraire » d'une proposition I (« Some pains are difficult to hide »). Dans le carré logique traditionnel, la contrariété lie seulement A et E ; I n'a pas de contraire. Lecture retenue : la proposition universelle de qualité opposée (E, « No pains are difficult to hide ») dont la converse simple est « No things that are difficult to hide are pains » ; la lecture par A (converse par limitation) est signalée dans le corrigé. Le barème attendu par le jury n'est pas connu.

Q1(a)(iv) : a(ii) est lue comme la proposition A « All pains are difficult to hide » (contradictoire de la sous-contraire de I). Fausse : sa contradictoire O est vraie, sa subalterne I est indéterminée (règles traditionnelles de la subalternation, avec import existentiel).

Q1(c) : les deux conséquents de la proposition du coach étant identiques (mourir sur le terrain), le dilemme construit à partir d'elle seule est de forme simple (D v D se réduit à D). Une variante à conséquents distincts (K v D), construite avec la proposition « If he shows any sign of pain, then he will be kicked out of the team », est donnée dans le corrigé. « Escaping between the horns » est lu comme la négation de la prémisse disjonctive.

Q1(d) : plusieurs sophismes sont défendables (fausse analogie dans la réponse de Chris, faux dilemme dans la phrase du coach, non sequitur « That is why the coach had to notice it »). Choix retenu : fausse analogie, la plus nette ; les autres sont mentionnés dans le corrigé.

Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR questions, choosing TWO questions from each Section imperatively » (quatre questions au total, deux par section). Section One (Logic) : questions 1 à 3 ; Section Two (Philosophical Problems) : questions 4 à 6. `regles_choix` porte une règle `parmi 2 sur 3` par section ; la règle « 4 en tout » est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « 25 marks ». Les points par sous-question sont la somme des points imprimés en marge de leurs parties (Q1 : 7 + 6 + 7 + 5 ; Q2 : 6 + 7 + 6 + 6 ; Q3 : 9 + 9 + 6 + 1), soit 25 par question : aucun écart. Les critères de la page de garde (introduction 5, thèse 7, antithèse 6, synthèse 3, conclusion 4) valent pour les dissertations de la Section Two.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées ; la logique est recalculée avec Python, la philosophie est donnée de mémoire (auteurs et positions de l'histoire établie de la philosophie, sans citation littérale, titre d'ouvrage, date ni numéro de page). À faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné de 3 pages (page de garde, puis Section One pages 2 et 3, Section Two en bas de la page 3) avec filigrane gcerevision.com, sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. questions.enonce_markdown:
(a)

(i) Bring out a Particular Affirmative Proposition from the passage above. (1 mark)

(ii) What is the Contradictory of the Sub-Contrary of a)(i) above? (2 marks)

(iii) Bring out very clearly the Converse of the Contrary of a(i) above (2 marks)

(iv) Given a(ii) above as False, what is the truth value of its contradictory and sub-alternation? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Particular affirmative proposition (1 mark).** A particular affirmative proposition is an **I** proposition, of the form "Some S are P". The passage contains one: **"Some pains are difficult to hide."** (S = pains; P = things that are difficult to hide.)

**(ii) Contradictory of the sub-contrary (2 marks).**
- The sub-contrary of an I proposition is the **O** proposition with the same subject and predicate: "Some pains are not difficult to hide."
- The contradictory of an O proposition is the **A** proposition (the two differ in both quantity and quality, so they can be neither both true nor both false).
- Answer: **"All pains are difficult to hide."** (A)

**(iii) Converse of the contrary (2 marks).** Strictly, contrariety holds only between A and E propositions, so an I proposition has no contrary of its own: its opposites on the square are O (sub-contrary), E (contradictory) and A (its superaltern). The question can therefore only mean the universal proposition that opposes a(i) in quality, namely the **E** proposition:
- E: "No pains are difficult to hide."
- Conversion of an E proposition is simple (subject and predicate are exchanged, quality and quantity unchanged), so the converse is: **"No things that are difficult to hide are pains."**

(If the examiner meant the universal affirmative A, "All pains are difficult to hide", its converse by limitation is "Some things that are difficult to hide are pains".)

**(iv) Truth values (2 marks).** a(ii) is the A proposition "All pains are difficult to hide", given as **False**.
- Its **contradictory** is the O proposition "Some pains are not difficult to hide". Contradictories always have opposite truth values, so it is **True**.
- Its **subaltern** (sub-alternation) is the I proposition "Some pains are difficult to hide". Truth passes down from A to I and falsity passes up from I to A, but the falsity of A tells us nothing about I, so its truth value is **undetermined (doubtful)**. (The passage itself states the I proposition, but that comes from the text, not from the rule of subalternation.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Use a suitable Hypothetical proposition found in the passage above to construct:

(i) A Modus Tollens (3 marks)

(ii) A Modus Ponens (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The hypothetical proposition.** The passage contains: "If he shows any sign of pain, then he will be kicked out of the team." Let $p$ = Chris shows a sign of pain; $q$ = Chris is kicked out of the team. The proposition is $p \supset q$.

**(i) Modus Tollens (3 marks)** (deny the consequent, therefore deny the antecedent: $p \supset q,\ \sim q \ \therefore\ \sim p$):

- If Chris shows any sign of pain, then he will be kicked out of the team.
- Chris is not kicked out of the team.
- Therefore, Chris does not show any sign of pain.

**(ii) Modus Ponens (3 marks)** (affirm the antecedent, therefore affirm the consequent: $p \supset q,\ p \ \therefore\ q$):

- If Chris shows any sign of pain, then he will be kicked out of the team.
- Chris shows a sign of pain.
- Therefore, Chris will be kicked out of the team.

Both are valid forms. Do not confuse them with the two fallacies built on the same conditional: affirming the consequent ("he was kicked out, so he showed pain") and denying the antecedent ("he showed no pain, so he will not be kicked out").

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c)

(i) Identify a suitable proposition in the passage that can be used to build up a Constructive Dilemma (1 mark)

(ii) Use the proposition in c(i) above to construct a Complex Constructive Dilemma (3 marks)

(iii) Refute c(ii) above by "Escaping between the horns". (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The proposition (1 mark).** The coach's statement is a conjunction of two hypothetical propositions:

"If he stays and plays then he will die in the field **and** if he fails to see the doctor then he will die in the field."

Let $S$ = Chris stays and plays; $F$ = Chris fails to see the doctor; $D$ = Chris will die in the field. The proposition is $(S \supset D) \cdot (F \supset D)$.

**(ii) The dilemma (3 marks).** A constructive dilemma combines a conjunction of two conditionals with a disjunction of their antecedents and concludes with a disjunction of their consequents: $(A \supset B) \cdot (C \supset D),\ A \vee C \ \therefore\ B \vee D$. With the coach's proposition:

- Major premise: If Chris stays and plays, he will die in the field, and if he fails to see the doctor, he will die in the field. $(S \supset D) \cdot (F \supset D)$
- Minor premise: Either Chris stays and plays or he fails to see the doctor. $S \vee F$
- Conclusion: Therefore, he will die in the field or he will die in the field, that is, he will die in the field. $D \vee D$

Because the two consequents are identical here, the conclusion collapses into the single proposition $D$ (the "simple" form of the dilemma). To obtain a conclusion with two different consequents (the "complex" form), the second conditional of the passage can be paired with the first one: $(P \supset K) \cdot (F \supset D)$, with $P$ = Chris shows a sign of pain and $K$ = he is kicked out of the team; minor premise "Either Chris shows a sign of pain or he fails to see the doctor" ($P \vee F$); conclusion "Therefore, either he will be kicked out of the team or he will die in the field" ($K \vee D$).

**(iii) Escaping between the horns (3 marks).** The two "horns" are the two conditionals (stay and play, with death; fail to see the doctor, with death). To escape between them is to show that the disjunctive premise $S \vee F$ is not exhaustive: there is a third alternative, so Chris need not take either horn. Chris can **neither stay and play nor fail to see the doctor**: he can see the doctor and be treated and rest (not playing), or ask the coach to replace him. Then $\sim S \cdot \sim F$ is true, the disjunction $S \vee F$ is false, and the dilemma, although formally valid, has a false premise and therefore proves nothing: its conclusion is not established.

(The other two refutations are different: "grasping the dilemma by the horns" denies one conditional, for instance by saying that playing does not necessarily lead to death; "rebutting" builds a counter-dilemma with an opposite conclusion.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d)

(i) Identify the Fallacy most clearly committed in the passage (2 marks)

(ii) Explain how the Fallacy in d(i) above has been committed (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The fallacy (2 marks).** The fallacy most clearly committed is the **fallacy of false (faulty) analogy**, in Chris's reply: "if Jones can play with a broken leg, so can I".

**(ii) Explanation (3 marks).** An argument from analogy has the form: Jones has property $a$ and can play with a broken leg; Chris resembles Jones in $a$; therefore Chris can also play in that condition. It is only strong if the two cases are alike in the respects that are relevant to the conclusion. Here:

- Chris concludes from a single case ("Jones") without any evidence that Jones really played well, safely, or for how long;
- the relevant factors differ or are unknown: the nature and seriousness of the injury, the person's pain tolerance and the medical risk. Chris could not even get up because the pain was "very sharp", and the coach warns that playing could kill him;
- the only similarity is that both are footballers who are hurt, which is not enough to show that the same outcome holds for Chris.

So the conclusion does not follow, because a relevant difference is ignored: the analogy is false.

(Other weaknesses are present: the coach's alternative "stay and play or fail to see the doctor" is a false dilemma, and "Some pains are difficult to hide. That is why the coach had to notice it" is a non sequitur. The analogy is the clearest because it is stated as an argument.)
